z-m-28-01.title: The solution that says 'there are 4000 passwords containing a 7': what looks off?
z-m-28-01.topic: The error in a solution that counts the cases 'containing a 7' in 4-digit passwords where repeats are allowed
z-m-28-01.goal: Using small cases, check why a solution that first picks a place and then fills in the rest counts the same password several times, and write how to find the correct count.
z-m-28-01.material: There is a 4-digit password made of the digits 0 to 9. Any digit from 0 to 9 can come in each place, the same digit may be used several times, and 0 may come in the first place (example: 0707). Below is the process by which Seoyun solved 'How many passwords contain the digit 7 at least once?' (This problem has nothing to do with real passwords.)
z-m-28-01.thinking.0: Examining, line by line, what object each line of a solution counts
z-m-28-01.thinking.1: Testing a solution by listing small cases directly
z-m-28-01.thinking.2: Judging whether the same object is counted several times
z-m-28-01.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-01.prereq.1: The habit of listing many cases directly and counting them
z-m-28-01.s.s1.prompt: Which line of Seoyun's solution makes the same password get counted several times? Lines are counted from 1.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.hint.0: Follow, with examples, 'which passwords' each line counts. How many times is 0770, which has two 7s, counted in this solution?
z-m-28-01.s.s1.hint.1: When picking one place in line 2, compare what happens if a 7 comes again in the other three places of line 3.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.0: The password has 4 places, each place can have 0 to 9, and the same digit may repeat. The total is 10×10×10×10=10000 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.1: To count passwords containing a 7, pick one place where the 7 will be placed. There are 4 places, so 4 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.2: Put a 7 in that place, and the other three places can have any digit, so 10×10×10=1000 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.3: So the number of passwords containing a 7 is 4×1000=4000 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.line.4: 4000 is less than the total 10000, so the value is reasonable.
z-m-28-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 3 together create the problem. If line 2 picks 'one place for the 7' and line 3 lets a 7 come again in the other three places, then a password with two or more 7s is counted once for each way of choosing the place. For example, 7777 is counted 4 times and 0770 is counted 2 times. Line 5 is also not a valid reason. The fact that a value is less than the total does not make that value right.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.prompt: To test the solution, I reduced the number of places and applied the same method to 2-digit passwords (00 to 99) (2 places for the 7 × 10 ways for the other place). What can we learn by comparing this value with the value from listing and counting directly those containing a 7 from 00 to 99?
z-m-28-01.s.s2.hint.0: Among 00 to 99, list separately those with 7 in the first place and those with 7 in the second place.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.hint.1: Look for passwords that are in both lists.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.a: The two values are the same. If it is right for 2 places, this method can be trusted.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that trusts the method without listing the small case directly. Only by listing and comparing do the method's flaws show.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.b: The method's value is larger. A number like 77 is counted twice.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.b: This thought compared the listed table with what the method counts and pointed out which passwords are counted twice.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.c: The method's value is smaller. This method leaves out some passwords.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.c: You noticed the values are different, but could not tell leaving out from double counting. If you match them one by one with the directly listed table, you can tell which it is.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.o.d: The two values differ. But as the number of places grows, that difference goes away.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.r.d: You did not check that as the number of places grows, passwords with several 7s become more numerous, so the difference does not go away.
z-m-28-01.s.s2.explain: Listing 2 places directly gives the 10 from 70 to 79 and the 10 of 07, 17, ..., 97, but 77 is in both, so there are 19. The method's value is 2×10=20, which counts 77 twice, once as 'first place is 7' and once as 'second place is 7.' For 4 places there are more passwords with two or more 7s, so the difference is larger.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.prompt: Write one correct way to find the number of 4-digit passwords containing a 7 at least once, and find the value. Also explain in one sentence how Seoyun's method counts a password like 7777 several times.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.hint.0: Count directly how many times passwords with several 7s, like 7777 or 0770, are counted in Seoyun's method.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.hint.1: First count how many passwords have no 7 at all, and think about how that value is related to this problem.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the value you got by your method also matches the directly listed value in a small case like 2 places?
z-m-28-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain 'counts several times' with one specific password like 7777?
z-m-28-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you choose one of the method of splitting by how many 7s there are and the method of using the case with no 7, and calculate it to the end?
z-m-28-01.s.s3.model.0: 7777 is counted once in each of the 4 ways of choosing the place for the 7, so it is counted 4 times. Excluding the 9×9×9×9=6561 ways with no 7 from all 10000 ways gives 3439 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.modelNote.0: An answer counted by the complement
z-m-28-01.s.s3.model.1: After the place is chosen, if a 7 goes into the others again, the same password is counted again. So we split by the number of 7s and add. Adding 4×729 for one 7, 6×81 for two, 4×9 for three, and 1 for four gives 3439 ways.
z-m-28-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer counted by splitting into cases

z-m-28-02.title: Two numbers came out for 'the number of ways to choose 3 out of 10'
z-m-28-02.topic: The number of cases, which changes with the purpose of choosing (whether roles are told apart)
z-m-28-02.goal: Realize that even for a problem with the same sentence, the answer differs depending on what you count as different cases, and find the information to check before deciding the answer.
z-m-28-02.material: From 10 students in the broadcasting club, 3 will be chosen to run an event. One person cannot take two positions. Chaemin said '720 ways' and Doha said '120 ways,' and neither of them made a calculation mistake. The two different values came out because there is something the problem has not yet told us.
z-m-28-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-28-02.thinking.1: Stating the standard for telling apart what is counted
z-m-28-02.thinking.2: Working out how the answer changes when the conditions change
z-m-28-02.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-02.prereq.1: Experience thinking about the standard that separates 'the same case' from 'a different case' in counting
z-m-28-02.s.s1.prompt: To decide which of the two values is right, what must you find out first?
z-m-28-02.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate 720÷120, and find out whether that number equals the count of something you can count using three fixed people A, B, and C.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how many times each of the two people would have counted one case in which A, B, and C are chosen.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.a: Whether the 3 chosen people take different roles
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.a: This is an attitude of asking whether even the same three people make a different case if their roles differ. It is checking first what to treat as the same case.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.b: Whether the 3 people are chosen one at a time in turn or all at once
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.b: This thought sees the choosing procedure as itself the distinction of order. You could also see that if the same three people are chosen, the result is the same no matter the procedure.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.c: How many of the 10 are third-years
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.c: The makeup of the grades could matter if more conditions were added, but it has nothing to do with why the two present values differ. First you must find where the two values split.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.o.d: Whether the same person can be chosen twice
z-m-28-02.s.s1.r.d: The problem already says one person takes only one position. This is asking about a given condition again.
z-m-28-02.s.s1.explain: Think of one case in which the three people A, B, and C are chosen. If there are no roles, that is the end of this one case, but if they take different roles, it splits into 6 ways depending on who has which role. 720 is 6 times 120. So 'whether roles are told apart' is the information that splits the two values.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.prompt: Then what situation is each of 720 and 120 the answer to? Write one sentence for each of the two situations as an actual event situation.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine and write one situation where all three people do the same work at the event, and one where the work they take on is different.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.hint.1: In each situation, write whether choosing A, B, and C is treated as the same case or a different case.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write, in your own words and specifically, what kind of 'distinction' each number comes from?
z-m-28-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain how many times one case is counted, using the same three people A, B, and C as an example?
z-m-28-02.s.s2.model.0: Choosing 3 people to do the same work without dividing roles gives 120 ways, and deciding different roles such as president, vice president, and secretary gives 720 ways. There are 6 ways to divide roles among the same three people, so 720 is 6 times 120.
z-m-28-02.s.s2.model.1: If the 3 people are one team and we don't tell apart who is in which seat, it is 120. If we tell apart the positions like 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place, even the same three people make a different case when the order differs, so it is 720.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.prompt: This is new information. Among the 3 chosen people, 1 is the 'team leader' and the other 2 are 'team members' who do the same work. How many ways are there to choose 1 team leader and 2 team members from 10 people?
z-m-28-02.s.s3.hint.0: Choose the three people first, and then work out how many ways there are to decide who among them is the team leader.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether you get the same value if you count in the order of deciding the team leader first and then choosing the team members from the rest.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.a: This counts the three people without telling them apart even though there is a team leader. It failed to account for the cases that differ depending on who the team leader is.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.b: This even tells apart the two team members from each other. The team members do the same work, so swapping them gives the same case.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.c: This sets the team leader and counts only one team member. It missed the condition that there are 2 team members.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.r.d: This is a judgment that, in a situation where only some are told apart, counts only as much as is told apart.
z-m-28-02.s.s3.explain: If you choose the three people first, it is 120 ways, and there are 3 ways to choose the team leader among them, so 120×3=360. Counting by deciding the team leader first (10 ways) and then 2 team members out of the remaining 9 (36 ways) also gives 10×36=360. Dividing 720 by the order of the two team members (2 ways) gives the same value.

z-m-28-03.title: The number of different arrangements when there are identical letter cards: comparing three solutions
z-m-28-03.topic: Arrangements with identical letter cards mixed in: comparing three different solutions
z-m-28-03.goal: Examine the validity of different solutions for the number of arrangements when identical-looking objects are mixed in, and work out the reason for the steps that multiply or divide.
z-m-28-03.material:
There are 6 letter cards. 3 are A, 2 are N, and 1 is B, and cards with the same letter look exactly alike, so they cannot be told apart. Three people solved differently for the number of different letter arrangements (example: BANANA, ABNANA) that can be made by putting the 6 cards in a row.
Seoha: There are 3 kinds of letters, so the way to line up 3 things is 3×2×1=6 ways.
Harin: If we treat all 6 as different, it is 720 ways. Swapping identical letters gives the same arrangement, so divide by the 6 orders of the 3 A cards and the 2 orders of the 2 N cards: 720÷12=60 ways.
Junho: There are 20 ways to choose the 3 places out of 6 for A. Among the remaining 3 places, there are 3 ways to choose the 2 places for N. B goes in the remaining place, so 20×3=60 ways.
z-m-28-03.thinking.0: Comparing several solutions to judge their validity
z-m-28-03.thinking.1: Examining the reason for each multiplication or division in the lines of a solution
z-m-28-03.thinking.2: Carrying a method over to new conditions
z-m-28-03.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-03.prereq.1: The number of ways to put n different things in a row
z-m-28-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the solutions that correctly find the number of different arrangements.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write out directly a few different arrangements like BANANA and ABNANA, and check whether all of them are included in the 6 ways that Seoha counted.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.hint.1: Fix B at the front, list and count directly the arrangements of the rest A A A N N in a row, and compare with the value each solution counted.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.r.a: This interpreted 'the cards cannot be told apart' as 'line up only the kinds of letters.' You need to check by writing out whether the fact that there are 3 A cards and 2 N cards is reflected in the arrangement.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.r.b: This solution counts as if all 6 are different and then divides by the amount from swapping identical ones. It counted how many times each object is repeated.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.r.c: This is a method that decides the places first and then puts in the letters. It is a judgment that, for identical letter cards, you only need to decide the places, so there is no need to count their order separately.
z-m-28-03.s.s1.explain: Harin's solution divides because the 720 ways when the 6 cards are told apart were counted 3!×2!=12 times for each same arrangement, and Junho's solution decides first the places where the letters go, so both solutions give the same 60 ways. Seoha's solution does not count the 6 cards being placed in a row and only lines up the kinds of letters. For example, BANANA and BNAANA cannot be told apart by the order of letter kinds alone.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.prompt: Minjae found, by the same method, the number of different arrangements of 'A 2 cards, B 2 cards, C 1 card' in a row. Which line of the solution is wrong? Lines are counted from 1.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.hint.0: For each line, write whether it makes the value larger or smaller than 120.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.hint.1: Starting from line 1, compare whether the same reason was applied between the 2 A cards and the 2 B cards.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.0: If the 5 cards are all different, it is 5×4×3×2×1=120 ways.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.1: Swapping the A cards gives the same arrangement, so divide by the 2 orders of the 2 A cards. 120÷2=60 ways.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.2: Swapping the B cards also gives the same arrangement, but this time the 2 orders of the 2 B cards are multiplied, giving 60×2=120 ways.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.line.3: So the number of different arrangements is 120 ways.
z-m-28-03.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. Swapping the same B cards also gives the same arrangement, so you must divide by 2, exactly as for A. 120÷2÷2=30 ways. When identical cards are mixed in, the number of different arrangements has to be smaller than the 120 ways when all cards are different, and Minjae's result did not get smaller than 120, which also shows something is odd.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.prompt: How many different arrangements are there in all of A 2 cards, B 2 cards, and C 2 cards in a row?
z-m-28-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write how many times the same arrangement is repeated for the 2 A cards, for the 2 B cards, and for the 2 C cards.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.hint.1: First count the ways to choose the places for the two A cards among the 6 places, then count the ways to choose the places for B among the remaining places, and compare.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.a: This is a judgment that found the value when all 6 are different and then divided by all the repetitions arising from each kind of card.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.b: This divided only by the order of the 2 A cards. You need to check whether swapping the identical B and C cards also gives the same arrangement.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.c: This is the value from lining up only the kinds of letters. The fact that there are 2 of each card was not used in the arrangement.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.r.d: This is a value where division was done twice and one was left out. Check whether the same reason applies to all three kinds.
z-m-28-03.s.s3.explain: 720÷(2×2×2)=90. Using the method of deciding places, C(6,2)×C(4,2)×C(2,2)=15×6×1=90 too (read: the product of the ways to choose 2 places for A among 6 places and 2 places for B among the remaining 4).

z-m-28-04.title: Ways to color a five-region map: as information is added, the estimate changes
z-m-28-04.topic: The number of ways to color adjacent regions in different colors (a middle region and a ring-shaped set of regions)
z-m-28-04.goal: When the neighbor conditions become known step by step, revise the estimated value, split into cases to find the exact value, and then apply it to a situation where the number of colors changes.
z-m-28-04.material: An imaginary island is divided into five regions A, B, C, D, and E. A is in the middle, and B, C, D, and E surround A. B and C, C and D, D and E, and E and B touch. B and D do not touch each other, and C and E do not touch each other. Touching at only one point does not count as touching. Regions that touch must be colored in different colors, and you do not have to use all the colors.
z-m-28-04.thinking.0: Fixing an estimate according to information
z-m-28-04.thinking.1: Finding where the neighbor conditions overlap and splitting into cases
z-m-28-04.thinking.2: Applying to a situation where the conditions have changed
z-m-28-04.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-04.prereq.1: Experience working out how many colors each region can be painted
z-m-28-04.s.s1.prompt: Each time information is added, estimate the number of ways to color and revise it.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.hint.0: Separate what you can say with the information you know now from what you have not yet been able to check.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.hint.1: When coloring one region, count how many of the regions touching it are already colored.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.info: There are 4 colors: red, yellow, green, and blue. First, one color was decided for A. A touches all of B, C, D, and E.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many colors are B, C, D, and E each limited to?
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.after: They touch A, so B, C, D, and E cannot use A's color. So they are chosen from 3 colors.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The condition of touching A was not used.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The 3 colors other than A's color
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This applied the condition that regions touching A must have a color different from A.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This limited the four regions to only two different colors. Any color different from A's can be used.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It seems to assume that B, C, D, and E all have the same color.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Suppose we color starting with B. I thought of 3 ways for B, 2 ways for C different from B because it touches B, and 2 ways for D different from C because it touches C. Now E touches both D and B.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How can we estimate the number of ways to color B, C, D, and E?
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.after: 3×2×2×2=24 is the value when you see 'E touches only D.' E also touches B, so the actual value is less than 24. So to find the number exactly, you have to split into cases by whether B and D have the same color or different colors.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a value that used none of the neighbor conditions.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a value counted as if E also touches only an earlier region. E touches two regions.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is an estimate that took into account the restriction arising from E touching two neighbors.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This estimate is too small. It is a judgment that once one region is decided, the rest are fixed to one.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Including the 4 colors for A, how many ways are there in all to color the whole map with 4 colors?
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This multiplied the 4 ways for A by the intermediate estimate 24 as it is.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This multiplied the 4 ways for A by 81, which has no neighbor conditions.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This counted only the ways to color B to E and did not multiply by the 4 colors for A.
z-m-28-04.s.s1.reflect: The first judgment (B to E use only 3 colors) held to the end. What changed was the intermediate estimate. 24 was the value that assumed 'there is only one neighbor,' so when the information that E touches two neighbors was added, it was corrected by the judgment that it must be smaller. Look back at whether finding where the estimate went off was more important than calculating.
z-m-28-04.s.s2.prompt: If we reduce the colors to 3 (red, yellow, green), how many ways are there to color the whole map? Write the value and the reason.
z-m-28-04.s.s2.hint.0: First write how many colors are left for B to E once A's color is decided.
z-m-28-04.s.s2.hint.1: Decide one color for B and color C, D, and E in turn, and check whether any choices arise.
z-m-28-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that only the two colors other than A's color remain?
z-m-28-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why, once one of B to E is decided, the rest are decided (colored in alternation)?
z-m-28-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you compare it with the method for 4 colors?
z-m-28-04.s.s2.model.0: Color A in 3 ways, and B to E can use only the remaining two colors. Neighboring regions must differ, so once B is decided, C, D, and E are decided alternately, and B has only 2 ways. 3×2=6 ways.
z-m-28-04.s.s2.model.1: Decide A's color in 3 ways. If B is colored with one of the remaining two colors, C must differ from B so it is the other color, D must differ from C so it has the same color as B, and E, for the same reason, has the same color as C. It is decided by B's 2 ways, so 3×2=6 ways.

z-m-28-05.title: Testing the claim 'with 10 points, there are always 120 triangles'
z-m-28-05.topic: Triangles made from 10 points on a plane: when some points are on a straight line
z-m-28-05.goal: Find the condition under which the claim holds, build arrangements that break the condition to find the number of triangles, and explain how the number changes.
z-m-28-05.material: There are 10 points on a plane. A triangle with three points as vertices is made only when those three points are not on one straight line. Triangles with the same vertices are counted as the same triangle. Jihu said, 'With 10 points, there are always 120 triangles.' Think about the arrangement below. Among the 10 points, k points (3 or more) are on one straight line, and apart from that there are no three points on one straight line.
z-m-28-05.thinking.0: Finding the condition under which a claim holds
z-m-28-05.thinking.1: Building a counterexample and finding its value
z-m-28-05.thinking.2: Explaining how the result changes as a variable changes
z-m-28-05.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-05.prereq.1: The fact that three points on one straight line do not make a triangle
z-m-28-05.s.s1.prompt: How is it right to judge Jihu's claim?
z-m-28-05.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine that 4 points are on one straight line and the other 6 are off that line, and work out which three of those 4 points can make a triangle.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write what condition is needed for the number of ways to choose three points to equal the number of triangles.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.a: It is always 120. With 10 points, the number of ways to choose three points is fixed.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.a: This assumed the number of ways to choose three points and the number of triangles are equal. It did not check whether the chosen three points always form a triangle.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.b: Depending on the arrangement, it can be more than 120. Because one point is used in several triangles.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.b: This misunderstood the fact that one point is used in several triangles as a reason to count more. A triangle is determined by the choice of three points, so the number of choices is the upper limit.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.c: Depending on the positions, it can be fewer than 120. Three points on a straight line are not a triangle.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.c: This found the condition under which the claim holds, in that some ways of choosing three points may not form a triangle.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.o.d: We can't tell. Until I see the positions of the points in a picture, I can't say anything.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.r.d: Even without a picture, you can test the claim by fixing the positions in words and building an arrangement.
z-m-28-05.s.s1.explain: The ways to choose three points are C(10,3)=120 (read: the number of ways to choose 3 from 10), but among them three points on a straight line are not a triangle. So if there are no three points on a straight line, it is 120, and if there are, it is fewer than 120. The condition that no three points are on a straight line is needed.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.prompt: In an arrangement where k of the 10 points are on one straight line, decide k, find the number of triangles t that can be made, and build 3 examples with different k. (k is from 3 to 10)
z-m-28-05.s.s2.hint.0: If k=3, first write how many triangles cannot be made from the three points on a straight line.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.hint.1: When k is 4 and 5, list and count directly how many ways there are to choose three points among the points on one straight line.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.var.k: The number of points on one straight line, k
z-m-28-05.s.s2.ok.c1: k is a natural number from 3 to 10.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make k a natural number from 3 to 10.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of triangles t is right.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.fail.c2: t is not right. Think again about how you handled the cases of choosing three points from the k points on one straight line.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.ok.c3: It is fewer than 120, so it is a counterexample to Jihu's claim.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.fail.c3: t is 120. To be a counterexample, it must be a value less than 120.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.explain: k=3 gives 119, k=4 gives 116, k=5 gives 110, and k=6 gives 100. The number of ways to choose three points from the k points on a straight line is k(k−1)(k−2)/6, and these do not form triangles, so subtract them from 120. Counting separately and adding the triangles that include 0, 1, or 2 points on the line gives the same value (k=4: 20+60+36=116).
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.prompt: As k gets larger, how does the number of triangles t change? Write the reason briefly.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare k and t in the two examples you made earlier.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about how many more choices of three points that do not form a triangle appear when k goes up by 1.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you state the direction of the change and give one numerical example with it?
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give the reason that three points on a straight line are not a triangle?
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.model.0: As k gets larger, t gets smaller. When the points on one straight line increase, the cases of choosing three points among them do not form triangles, so the cases that must be subtracted keep growing.
z-m-28-05.s.s2.because.model.1: It gets smaller: 119 when k=3, 116 when k=4, 110 when k=5. Points on a straight line cannot make a triangle even if you choose them three at a time, and such choices of three points increase as k gets larger.

z-m-28-06.title: A solution that came out to 0: at which line did it go wrong?
z-m-28-06.topic: Among the triangles made from the vertices of a regular octagon, the number of triangles that use no side of the octagon
z-m-28-06.goal: Check with a small example that the result is impossible, find the first line that went wrong and fix it, and find the correct count.
z-m-28-06.material: The vertices of a regular octagon are numbered 1, 2, ..., 8 in the clockwise direction. When we make triangles with 3 of them as vertices, how many triangles have none of their three sides being a side of the octagon (all three sides are diagonals of the octagon)? Vertex 8 is next to vertex 1, and a segment joining neighboring vertices is a side of the octagon. Doha's solution is as follows.
z-m-28-06.thinking.0: Checking whether the result makes sense
z-m-28-06.thinking.1: Finding the wrong line in a solution that splits into cases
z-m-28-06.thinking.2: Checking by building examples with the fixed solution
z-m-28-06.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-06.prereq.1: Telling apart the sides and the diagonals of a polygon
z-m-28-06.s.s1.prompt: Doha's conclusion is 0. At which line is the first mistake in the solution? Lines are counted from 1.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many sides of the octagon are used if you choose vertices 1, 3, and 5, and compare with Doha's conclusion.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.hint.1: In line 3, when side 1-2 is chosen, write the '6 vertices other than the two end points' directly, make a triangle with each one, and count how many sides of the octagon it has.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.0: There are 56 ways to choose 3 from 8 vertices, and the three chosen points always form a triangle.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.1: The triangles that use 2 sides of the octagon are the cases of choosing three neighboring vertices (for example, vertices 1, 2, 3), and there are 8 of them.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.2: A triangle that uses exactly 1 side of the octagon is found by choosing one side (8 ways) and choosing one of the 6 vertices other than that side's end points, so it is 8×6=48 ways.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.line.3: The triangles that use a side are 8+48=56 ways, so the triangles that use no side are 56−56=0 ways.
z-m-28-06.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first mistake. When side 1-2 is chosen, among the 6 vertices other than end points 1 and 2 are vertex 8 (next to 1) and vertex 3 (next to 2). Choosing either of these gives 2 sides, so it cannot be put into 'exactly 1.' The possible vertices are only the 4 vertices 4, 5, 6, and 7, so it is 8×4=32 ways. The conclusion of 0 is also strange. This is because choosing vertices 1, 3, and 5 gives a triangle that uses no side.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.prompt: To correct this, make 3 different triangles that use exactly one side of the octagon. The side used is the segment joining vertex p and vertex p+1 (if p is 8, vertex 8 and vertex 1), and the third vertex is vertex c.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.hint.0: The vertices next to side p-(p+1) are vertex (p−1) and vertex (p+2). Write directly the vertices left after excluding these two and p and p+1.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.hint.1: With the c you chose, write all three sides of the triangle and check one by one whether each is a side of the octagon.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.var.p: Starting vertex p of the side
z-m-28-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make p and c natural numbers from 1 to 8.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.ok.c2: Exactly one side of the octagon is used.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.fail.c2: With this c, exactly one side of the octagon is not used. Check whether c is an end point of the side or a vertex next to an end point.
z-m-28-06.s.s2.explain: If side 1-2 is chosen, c is one of the 4 vertices 4, 5, 6, and 7. There are 8 sides, so 8×4=32 ways. The triangles made of three neighboring vertices (2 sides) number 8, so the triangles that use at least one side are 32+8=40 ways, and the triangles that use no side are 56−40=16 ways.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.prompt: With the corrected calculation, how many triangles in all use no side (all three sides are diagonals)?
z-m-28-06.s.s3.hint.0: Split the total 56 into those that use 2 sides, those that use exactly 1, and those that use none, and organize them in a table.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.hint.1: Give directly a few examples of triangles made from three vertices that are not next to each other.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.a: This is the value counted by subtracting only the triangles that use 2 sides. It did not subtract the triangles that use exactly 1 side.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.b: This is the value from subtracting only the triangles that use exactly 1 side. The triangles that use 2 sides must be subtracted too.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.c: You trusted the result of the first solution as it was. It changes if you check the triangle made by 1, 3, and 5.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.r.d: This is a judgment that subtracted both the triangles that use 2 sides and the triangles that use exactly 1 side.
z-m-28-06.s.s3.explain: It is 56−8−32=16. These are the cases of choosing three vertices that are not next to each other, like 1, 3, and 5. Counting directly the ways to choose 3 of 8 points with no two next to each other also gives 16.

z-m-28-07.title: Interpreting the record that 22 and 25 applicants add up to 47
z-m-28-07.topic: Interpreting data that seems contradictory between the sum of the numbers of applicants for two activities and the total number of people
z-m-28-07.goal: Explain why the sum of the numbers of applicants can be greater than the total number of people, build the several possibilities the data allows, and judge what one more piece of information would fix the value.
z-m-28-07.material: 40 club students were asked to sign up for experience activities. 22 applied for swimming and 25 applied for hiking. One student can apply for both activities. The teacher in charge wrote down, 'The number of students who applied for swimming or hiking is 22+25=47.'
z-m-28-07.thinking.1: Building several possibilities that satisfy the constraints
z-m-28-07.thinking.2: Picking out the information that is needed
z-m-28-07.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-07.prereq.1: Experience counting numbers of students by dividing them into groups
z-m-28-07.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the record of 47 together with the 40 students, what is the most reasonable way to interpret it?
z-m-28-07.s.s1.hint.0: Work out how many times a student who applied for both swimming and hiking was counted in 22+25.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write one sentence each on what the 40 students and the 47 applications are counting.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.a: The application data is wrong. With 40 students, 47 cannot have applied.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.a: You missed the condition that one student can apply for both activities.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.b: 47−40=7, so 7 students did not apply for any activity.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.b: You interpreted the excess as non-applicants. The sum being larger than the total may rather be because of double applications.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.c: There are students who applied for both activities, so 47 is the number of applications, not the number of students.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.c: You thought of the possibility that a student was counted twice and interpreted the data and the condition together.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.o.d: The number of students may not be 40. 22+25 is right, so there are 47 students.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.r.d: You changed part of the data (40) to keep your conclusion. It is already given as 40.
z-m-28-07.s.s1.explain: If a student applied for both swimming and hiking, that student is counted twice in 22+25. So it is not strange for the sum to be greater than the total. 47 is not the number of students but the number of applications.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.prompt: Suppose all the data are right and each of the 40 students is one of: applied for swimming only, hiking only, both, or neither. Make 3 different possible pairs of the number b of students who applied for both activities and the number n of students who applied for neither.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.hint.0: Divide into four groups, swimming only, hiking only, both, and neither, and express the numbers of people using b and n.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.hint.1: If b of the 22 swimming applicants applied for both, write how many students applied for swimming only.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.var.b: Number of students who applied for both, b
z-m-28-07.s.s2.var.n: Number of students who applied for neither, n
z-m-28-07.s.s2.ok.c1: b and n are integers that are 0 or more.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make b and n integers that are 0 or more.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The students who applied for both are at most the 22 swimming applicants.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The students who applied for both cannot be more than the 22 swimming applicants.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The students who applied for at least one plus the students who applied for none add up to 40.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.fail.c3: (Number of students who applied for at least one)+(number of students who applied for neither) is not 40. Try expressing the number of students who applied for at least one using b.
z-m-28-07.s.s2.explain: b and n satisfy n=b−7 and 7≤b≤22. For example, (7, 0) is the case where everyone applied and 7 students overlap, and (22, 15) is the case where all 22 swimming applicants also applied for hiking and 15 students applied for nothing. The data alone do not fix a single pair.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.prompt: The teacher wants to settle the number of 'students who applied for swimming or hiking.' Choose all the pieces of information among the following such that being told just that one piece fixes the number.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, work out how many of the groups (swimming only, hiking only, both, neither) have their numbers fixed once that value is known.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.hint.1: Test one by one whether b can be found from the single value given in each option.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.o.a: Number of students who applied for swimming only
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.a: You recalled that subtracting the swimming-only students from the 22 swimming applicants fixes the overlapping students.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.o.b: Number of first-years among the students who applied
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.b: The number of people by grade does not tell how much the two activities overlapped.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.o.c: Number of students who applied for neither
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.c: You recalled that subtracting the students who did not apply from the total 40 immediately gives the number of students who applied.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.o.d: Number of students whose first application was for swimming
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.d: The order of applying has nothing to do with the overlap.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.o.e: Number of students who applied for both swimming and hiking
z-m-28-07.s.s3.r.e: You recalled that if you know the number of overlapping students, you can subtract the overlap from the sum.
z-m-28-07.s.s3.explain: If s students applied for swimming only, then 22−s students applied for both and the union is 25+s. If n students applied for neither, the union is 40−n. If b students applied for both, the union is 47−b. The distribution by grade or the order of applying does not fix the amount of overlap.

z-m-28-08.title: The number of ways to climb stairs: once a pattern shows up, can we trust it?
z-m-28-08.topic: The number of ways to climb 1 or 2 steps at a time (finding the pattern in the numbers and its reason)
z-m-28-08.goal: Realize that the pattern seen in the first few values is not fixed to one, find the reason for the pattern from the structure and extend the values, and check the same value by a different method.
z-m-28-08.material: You can climb 1 step or 2 steps at a time. When there are n steps, let a(n) be the number of different ways to climb from the very bottom to the very top (read it as 'a of n'). If the order of strides differs, it is a different way. For example, with 3 steps there are 3 ways, 1-1-1, 1-2, and 2-1, so a(3)=3.
z-m-28-08.thinking.0: Guessing a pattern from data alone and knowing its limits
z-m-28-08.thinking.1: Finding the reason for a pattern from the structure
z-m-28-08.thinking.2: Checking the same value by a different method
z-m-28-08.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-08.prereq.1: The convention that a different order of strides is a different way, and addition of natural numbers
z-m-28-08.s.s1.prompt: Each time information is added, estimate the value and revise it.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.hint.0: First write how many patterns you can state with the values you know now.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new information narrows the estimate down to one, or several still remain.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.after: From the three values 1, 2, 3 alone, both 'it goes up by one each time' (4) and 'the sum of the previous two values' (5) are possible. At this step it cannot be fixed to one.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: I saw 1, 2, 3 as continuing by going up by one each time.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: I saw it as adding the previous two values.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: I saw it as multiplying the previous two values. a(3)=3 does not fit this rule.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.0.r.d: I saw the values as doubling each time. This does not fit 1, 2, 3.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.info: Listing directly, a(4)=5 (1-1-1-1, 1-1-2, 1-2-1, 2-1-1, 2-2). The values became 1, 2, 3, 5.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.after: From 1, 2, 3, 5, both 'the differences are 1, 1, 2, so the next difference is 2' (7) and 'the sum of the previous two values' (8) seem natural. It is still hard to be sure from the numbers alone.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: I saw the 1 as continuing even after the differences 1, 1, 2.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: I saw a 2 coming after the differences 1, 1, 2.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: I saw the rule of adding the previous two values as continuing.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.1.r.d: I saw the values as doubling each time. This does not fit 1, 2, 3, 5.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.info: Work out the reason. The last stride just before arriving at the top is 1 step or 2 steps. If the last stride is 1 step, the ways of climbing up to n−1 steps before it are a(n−1), and if it is 2 steps, the ways of climbing up to n−2 steps are a(n−2). These two cases do not overlap.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: Using this structure, what are a(5) and a(8)?
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.after: a(5)=a(4)+a(3)=5+3=8, a(6)=13, a(7)=21, a(8)=34. Now that the reason is known from the structure, the estimate made from the numbers alone is confirmed.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: After getting 7 with the difference rule, I misread the numbering by one place and got 21.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: I extended the values using the structure that splits the cases by the last stride.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: I used the structure up to the 5th value, but after that I increased by 3 each time.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.st.2.r.d: I saw the values as increasing by 5 each time.
z-m-28-08.s.s1.reflect: At first both 4 and 5 (and then 7 and 8) were possible, but once the reason of splitting by whether the last stride is 1 step or 2 steps was known, it was fixed to one. Think about how settling on one just by looking at the pattern in the numbers differs from finding the reason and confirming.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 different ways to climb 8 steps in exactly 5 strides. Each stride is 1 step or 2 steps, and if the order of strides differs, it is a different way. (in order w1, w2, w3, w4, w5)
z-m-28-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide how many of the 5 strides must be 2-step strides for the sum to be 8.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.hint.1: After deciding the number of 2-step strides, change only the places where those strides come to make different orders.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.ok.c1: Each stride is 1 step or 2 steps.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the strides is not 8.
z-m-28-08.s.s2.explain: For the sum of 5 strides to be 8, there must be exactly three 2-step strides and two 1-step strides. So only the two places where the 1-step strides come differ, and there are 10 ways of choosing 2 of the 5 places.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.prompt: How many ways in all are there to climb 8 steps in exactly 5 strides?
z-m-28-08.s.s3.hint.0: For each of the cases of climbing 8 steps in 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 strides, write how many 2-step strides there are.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the sum of the values counted by number of strides equals the a(8) extended earlier.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.a: This counts only the cases where the place of the 2-step stride is changed by just one.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.b: This is a judgment counted by the method of choosing the places where the 1-step strides (or 2-step strides) come among the 5 strides.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.c: This is a value that told the order apart while choosing the places of the 2-step strides. The same choice of places was counted several times.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.r.d: This is the value of choosing 2 out of 6. The number of strides 5 was misread as 6.
z-m-28-08.s.s3.explain: If you choose from 5 places the places where the two 1-step strides come, all the rest are 2-step strides, so the number of ways to choose 2 of the 5 places is 10 ways. You can also check by splitting by number of strides and adding. 4 strides give 1 way, 5 strides give 10 ways, 6 strides give 15 ways, 7 strides give 7 ways, and 8 strides give 1 way, and the total 34 ways equals a(8)=34.

z-m-28-09.title: We found solutions with x<y<z; if we remove the order, how many solutions are there?
z-m-28-09.topic: Three different natural numbers with sum 12: a condition that fixes the order and a condition that does not
z-m-28-09.goal: Find the solutions that satisfy a condition systematically, and explain how fixing the order in the condition, and releasing it, affects the number of solutions.
z-m-28-09.material: Different natural numbers x, y, z satisfy x<y<z and x+y+z=12. The natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, ... For example, (1, 2, 9) satisfies the condition.
z-m-28-09.thinking.0: Building several solutions that satisfy the constraints
z-m-28-09.thinking.1: Choosing a method that finds all of them without missing any
z-m-28-09.thinking.2: Explaining the effect of the order condition on the count
z-m-28-09.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-09.prereq.1: Addition of natural numbers and comparing sizes
z-m-28-09.s.s1.prompt: Make 5 different (x, y, z) that satisfy the condition.
z-m-28-09.s.s1.hint.0: First fix the smallest x as 1, write what y+z is, and then look for pairs that satisfy y<z.
z-m-28-09.s.s1.hint.1: Organize the solutions you found in a table starting from the smallest x, and check that none are missing.
z-m-28-09.s.s1.ok.c1: x, y, and z are natural numbers.
z-m-28-09.s.s1.fail.c1: Please make x, y, and z natural numbers that are 1 or more.
z-m-28-09.s.s1.fail.c2: Please arrange the sizes so that x<y<z.
z-m-28-09.s.s1.explain: The solutions that satisfy the condition are the 7 solutions (1,2,9), (1,3,8), (1,4,7), (1,5,6), (2,3,7), (2,4,6), (3,4,5).
z-m-28-09.s.s2.prompt: What is the most suitable way to check that you found all of them without missing any?
z-m-28-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write the value of y+z for x=1, x=2, and x=3, and list the pairs with y<z.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.hint.1: Test whether there are solutions when x is 4, and decide where to stop.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.a: Set x as 1, 2, 3, ... and investigate the pairs with y<z.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.a: You used the fact that if you fix one variable in turn and investigate the rest, you can tell how far you have gone.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.b: Count only the values of x, thinking that once x is fixed, y and z are fixed to one.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.b: Even when x is 1 alone, there are several pairs of y and z. You assumed they are fixed to one.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.c: For each solution found, also add the ones with x, y, z swapped as new solutions and count them.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.c: The condition x<y<z has already fixed the order to one. The swapped ones break the condition, so they are not solutions.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.o.d: Start by fixing z as the largest value 12 and investigate while reducing x and y.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.r.d: If z is 12, then x+y=0, so there is no natural number solution. You did not consider the range when starting with the largest number.
z-m-28-09.s.s2.explain: If x is 1, then y+z=11 and there are 4 pairs with y<z; if x is 2, then y+z=10 and there are 2 pairs with y≥3; if x is 3, then y+z=9 and there is 1 pair with y≥4; and if x is 4 or more, there are no solutions. The total is 7.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.prompt: Now remove the condition x<y<z, and it is enough that x, y, z are different natural numbers with x+y+z=12 ((9, 1, 2) is also a solution). How many solutions are there in all? Write the value and the reason.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.hint.0: From the one solution (1, 2, 9) with x<y<z, write all the solutions you can make by swapping the places of the three numbers.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the solutions with swapped places are different solutions from each other, and whether they overlap with solutions from other groups.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in how many orders one group of three different numbers can be placed?
z-m-28-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason for multiplying all 7 groups by the same value (each group has the same 6 orders)?
z-m-28-09.s.s3.model.0: Each of the 7 solutions with x<y<z has 6 orders of lining up the three numbers, and since the three numbers are different, all are different solutions. So 7×6=42.
z-m-28-09.s.s3.model.1: The ways to place a group of three numbers like {1, 2, 9} into (x, y, z) number 3×2×1=6 each, so 42 in all for the 7 groups.

z-m-28-10.title: Is CBEAD the 58th or the 59th?
z-m-28-10.topic: Finding the position number of a word listed in dictionary order (alphabetical order)
z-m-28-10.goal: Check the relationship between 'the number of words before it' and 'which position it is' with a small case, judge which of the two people's calculations is valid, and apply it to the reverse problem (finding the word from the number).
z-m-28-10.material:
Using each of the five letters A, B, C, D, and E exactly once to make 5-letter words and listing them all in dictionary order (alphabetical order) gives 120 words. The first word is ABCDE, the second is ABCED, and the last is EDCBA. Jiwon and Taemin found which position the word 'CBEAD' is.
Jiwon: Count 24 words starting with A, 24 words starting with B, 6 words starting with C whose second letter is A, 2 words starting with CBA, and 2 words starting with CBD. 24+24+6+2+2=58, so it is the 58th.
Taemin: After counting the same words as Jiwon, he says it is the 59th.
z-m-28-10.thinking.0: Finding the difference between two calculations and judging
z-m-28-10.thinking.1: Testing a judgment with a small case
z-m-28-10.thinking.2: Applying the same structure to a problem in the opposite direction
z-m-28-10.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-10.prereq.1: The number of ways to line up n different things in a row (n!)
z-m-28-10.s.s1.prompt: Which of the two people's values, 58 or 59, do you judge to be right?
z-m-28-10.s.s1.hint.0: Group the words that come before CBEAD by starting letter in order and write how many there are in each group.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.a: Jiwon is right. The value counting the words before CBEAD is itself the position.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.a: This treats 'how many are before it' and 'which position it is' as the same. You did not check the relationship between the two with a small case.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.b: Both are wrong. All 24 words starting with C must come before it.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.b: You missed that only the words starting with C that come before CBEAD are counted.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.c: We can't tell. We can't settle it until we list all 120 words.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.c: If you count by sorting into groups, you can settle it without listing. You did not use the method of judging without listing.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.o.d: Taemin is right. There are 58 words before it, so it is the next one, the 59th.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.r.d: You judged based on the relationship between the number before and the position.
z-m-28-10.s.s1.explain: The words before CBEAD are 24 starting with A, 24 starting with B, 6 starting with CA, 2 starting with CBA, and 2 starting with CBD, 58 in all. CBEAD comes first of the two words starting with CBE (CBEAD, CBEDA), so it is the next one, the 59th. Jiwon's 58 is the number of words before CBEAD.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.prompt: Let's check with a small case. List in dictionary order the 6 words made by using each of the three letters A, B, and C once, and find which position CAB is. Write the relationship between that value and the number of words before CAB, and explain whose method is right.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write directly the 6 three-letter words in dictionary order.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.hint.1: Write side by side the number of words before CAB and the position of CAB, and compare them.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the 6 words in dictionary order without missing any?
z-m-28-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you show the difference between 'the number before it' and 'which position' with numbers?
z-m-28-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you connect that relationship to the case of CBEAD and judge the two people's values?
z-m-28-10.s.s2.model.0: The order is ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA, so CAB is the 5th. There are 4 before CAB, so the position is the number before it plus 1. So if there are 58 before CBEAD, it is the 59th, and Taemin is right.
z-m-28-10.s.s2.model.1: Writing the 6 words, CAB is the fifth. There are 4 words before it, so 'which position' counts up to the word itself and is 5. Jiwon gave the value counted without the word itself as the position.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.prompt: When the 120 five-letter words are listed in the same dictionary order, what is the 100th word?
z-m-28-10.s.s3.hint.0: Add up how many words start with each of A to D, and find from which position the words starting with E begin.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.hint.1: List directly the first four words starting with E from the front.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.r.a: It is the 99th word. It is an error in the same direction as the value you get when you confuse the number before with the position.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.r.b: I found it by the grouping that the words starting with E begin at the 97th and the 100th is the fourth among them.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.r.c: It is the 101st word. When deciding the position, it went off by 1 on the larger side.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.r.d: It is the 98th word. The calculation of which position it is among the words starting with E went off.
z-m-28-10.s.s3.explain: There are 24 words each starting with A, B, C, and D, 96 in all, so the words starting with E begin at the 97th. The 100th is the fourth among them, and the fourth in dictionary order of the remaining A, B, C, D is ACDB (in the order ABCD, ABDC, ACBD, ACDB), so it is EACDB.

z-m-28-11.title: Testing the claim 'there are only 3 tie cases'
z-m-28-11.topic: Rock-paper-scissors played by three people at once: counting cases split by result
z-m-28-11.goal: Test the claim with a counterexample, and split all the cases into non-overlapping result groups and count them to check that the sum matches the total.
z-m-28-11.material: Three people A, B, and C each show one of scissors, rock, or paper at the same time. Scissors beats paper, rock beats scissors, and paper beats rock. Write what the three people showed in the order (A, B, C) to tell the cases apart (example: (scissors, scissors, paper) and (scissors, paper, scissors) are different cases). The results are divided into three kinds. If what one person showed beats both of the other two, it is 'one wins'; if two people who showed the same thing beat the remaining one, it is 'two win'; otherwise it is a 'tie.' Eunwoo said, 'There are 27 in all, and a tie happens only when the three people show the same thing, so there are 3.'
z-m-28-11.thinking.0: Testing a claim with a counterexample
z-m-28-11.thinking.1: Building cases that satisfy a condition yourself
z-m-28-11.thinking.2: Splitting the whole into groups and checking the sum
z-m-28-11.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-11.prereq.1: Counting cases: telling different cases apart by writing them as ordered pairs
z-m-28-11.s.s1.prompt: How is it right to judge Eunwoo's statement?
z-m-28-11.s.s1.hint.0: When each person showed a different one of scissors, rock, and paper, write one by one who beats whom.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.hint.1: Look for cases among 'the three are not all the same' where no one wins.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.a: It is right. If the three people do not show the same thing, someone surely wins.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.a: You only looked at 'not the same' and did not examine the winning relationships. You need to write out directly who beats whom when the three people all show different things.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.b: It is wrong. The cases where the three people all show different things are also included in ties.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.b: You thought about how, when all three differ, no one beats both of the others, and came up with a counterexample.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.c: It is right. The number of cases the three people can show is 3×3×3, so ties are at most 3.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.c: You put an unfounded upper limit between the total number of cases and the number of tie cases.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.o.d: It is wrong. All the remaining 24 cases other than all-the-same are ties.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.r.d: You saw that there is a counterexample, but did not check whether the other cases also have winning results.
z-m-28-11.s.s1.explain: If all three show different things like (scissors, rock, paper), scissors beats paper but loses to rock, and no one beats both of the other two, so it is a tie. This kind of case is also included in ties, so Eunwoo's statement is wrong.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 different cases where two people who showed the same thing beat the remaining one ('two win'), like rock beating scissors. Write scissors as 1, rock as 2, and paper as 3.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.hint.0: The two winners showed the same thing. First decide what the two show, and then have the remaining person show what loses to it.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.hint.1: Scissors beats paper, rock beats scissors, and paper beats rock. Check how this relationship appears with the numbers 1, 2, 3.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose from scissors=1, rock=2, paper=3.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.ok.c2: Exactly two people showed the same thing.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.fail.c2: Exactly two people must show the same thing.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.ok.c3: The two who showed the same thing beat the remaining one.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.fail.c3: The two who showed the same thing do not beat the remaining one. Check the relationship that scissors beats paper, rock beats scissors, and paper beats rock.
z-m-28-11.s.s2.explain: The pair who showed the same thing can show 3 things, scissors, rock, or paper, and then what the remaining person shows is fixed. Which of A, B, and C is the loser has 3 possibilities, so it is 3×3=9 ways.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.prompt: If you split the 27 cases the three people can show into 'tie,' 'one wins,' and 'two win' and count them, what happens?
z-m-28-11.s.s3.hint.0: For the cases where one wins, work out how the rest is fixed once you decide who the winner is and what that person showed.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the sum of the three groups is 27 and whether any cases overlap or are missing.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.o.a: Tie 3 ways, one wins 12 ways, two win 12 ways
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.a: This keeps the first judgment (tie 3 ways) and splits the rest in half.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.o.b: Tie 6 ways, one wins 12 ways, two win 9 ways
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.b: This value left out the all-the-same cases from the ties.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.o.c: Tie 9 ways, one wins 9 ways, two win 9 ways
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.c: This is a judgment that counted by working out the ties (all the same 3 + all different 6) and the two winning groups separately.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.o.d: Tie 9 ways, one wins 6 ways, two win 12 ways
z-m-28-11.s.s3.r.d: The ties were counted correctly, but one of the two winning groups was counted wrongly and only the sum was made to match.
z-m-28-11.s.s3.explain: The ties are 3 ways with all the same plus 3×2×1=6 ways with all different, 9 ways. For 'one wins,' who among the 3 people is the winner and what the winner showed (3 possibilities) give 3×3=9 ways, and 'two win' is also 3×3=9 ways. The sum 9+9+9=27 equals the total number of cases.

z-m-28-12.title: Choosing a 4-person delegation: checking the same value by two routes
z-m-28-12.topic: Forming a delegation with a condition ('at least 1 from each grade'): checking by two methods
z-m-28-12.goal: Check a value found by finding and counting all the arrangements that satisfy the condition by a method that excludes the cases that do not fit the condition, and explain why the solution that counts overlapping is wrong.
z-m-28-12.material: A debate club has 5 first-years and 4 second-years. 4 of them will be chosen to form a delegation, and it must include at least 1 first-year and at least 1 second-year. The same 4 people make the same delegation, and roles within the delegation are not told apart.
z-m-28-12.thinking.0: Splitting the possible makeups without missing any
z-m-28-12.thinking.1: Checking the same value by different methods
z-m-28-12.thinking.2: Explaining the error of a solution that counts overlapping
z-m-28-12.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-12.prereq.1: The number of ways to choose r out of n without order (read: the number of ways to choose r out of n)
z-m-28-12.s.s1.prompt: Make 3 different possible grade makeups of the delegation that satisfy the condition (m first-years, w second-years). m+w is 4, and neither can exceed the number of people in each grade.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.hint.0: First decide how many second-years w must be when m is 1.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the condition is satisfied when m is 4 or more and when it is 0.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.ok.c1: m and w are integers that are 0 or more.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.fail.c1: Please make m and w integers that are 0 or more.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.fail.c2: Please make m and w add up to 4 people.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.fail.c3: If it is made up of only one grade, it does not fit the condition.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.ok.c4: Neither exceeds the number of people in each grade.
z-m-28-12.s.s1.fail.c4: It cannot exceed the number of people in each grade (5 first-years, 4 second-years).
z-m-28-12.s.s1.explain: The makeups are only these 3: (1 first-year, 3 second-years), (2, 2), (3, 1). If it is 4 first-years or 4 second-years, it is made up of only one grade and does not fit the condition.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.prompt: If you find the number of ways to choose the delegation for each makeup and add them all, how many ways is it?
z-m-28-12.s.s2.hint.0: For each makeup, write separately the number of ways to choose m from the 5 first-years and w from the 4 second-years.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether delegations of different makeups can be the same.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.r.b: This looks like a value counted by first fixing 1 person from each grade and then choosing the rest, but the same delegation was counted several times.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.r.c: This is the number of ways to choose 4 of 9 people with no condition. It did not exclude the cases made up of only one grade.
z-m-28-12.s.s2.explain: (1, 3) is 5×4=20 ways, (2, 2) is 10×6=60 ways, and (3, 1) is 10×4=40 ways, and the sum is 120 ways. Delegations of different makeups are different delegations, so they do not overlap.
z-m-28-12.s.s3.hint.0: Write separately by grade how many delegations are made up of only one grade.
z-m-28-12.s.s3.hint.1: Work out directly how many times the delegation made of first-years A and B and second-years C and D is counted in the wrong solution.
z-m-28-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write specifically what the cases that do not fit the condition are?
z-m-28-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give one example of how many times the same delegation is counted in the wrong solution?
z-m-28-12.s.s3.model.0: From the total 126 ways of choosing 4 of 9 people, subtract the 5 ways of choosing only first-years and the 1 way of choosing only second-years to get 120 ways. If you first fix one person from each grade and then choose the rest, the same delegation is counted several times, so it is wrong.
z-m-28-12.s.s3.model.1: The cases that do not fit the condition are the cases made up of only one grade: 5 ways for 4 first-years and 1 way for 4 second-years. Subtracting 6 ways from the total 126 ways gives 120 ways. If you first fix one first-year and one second-year, the same delegation is counted repeatedly.

z-m-28-13.title: Explaining C(10,3)=C(9,2)+C(9,3) to a friend without calculating
z-m-28-13.topic: An explanation that a number of combinations splits into two parts: the case where one particular person is chosen and the case where that person is not chosen
z-m-28-13.goal: Explain why the equation holds by sorting what is being counted, not by calculating, and carry the same explanation over to other numbers.
z-m-28-13.material: There is an equation: 'The number of ways to choose 3 out of 10 people, C(10,3), equals the number of cases where one particular person A is chosen, C(9,2), plus the number of cases where A is not chosen, C(9,3).' I know how to show by calculating that 120=36+84, but I want to know why it is true. Below is a short memo a friend wrote giving the reason. (Read C(9,2) as 'the number of ways to choose 2 out of 9 people.')
z-m-28-13.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in an explanation
z-m-28-13.thinking.1: Rewriting so the intended reader can understand
z-m-28-13.thinking.2: Carrying the same structure over to new numbers
z-m-28-13.prereq.0: We assume students who have already learned the counting-cases unit (sum rule, product rule, the meaning of permutations nPr and combinations nCr). 'H3' is the difficulty label of this set of tasks and does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade.
z-m-28-13.prereq.1: The meaning of the combination symbol C(n, r) (read: the number of ways to choose r out of n)
z-m-28-13.s.s1.prompt: Which line in the memo is the first one that is wrong? Lines are counted from 1.
z-m-28-13.s.s1.hint.0: Write, for the case where A is not chosen, out of how many people the 3 are chosen and how many are chosen.
z-m-28-13.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, check whether the numbers inside C( , ) match 'the number of remaining people' and 'the number of people still to choose.'
z-m-28-13.s.s1.line.0: Count all the cases of choosing 3 out of 10 people. Call one particular person A.
z-m-28-13.s.s1.line.1: Case where A is chosen: besides A, 2 more are chosen from the other 9, so there are C(9,2) ways.
z-m-28-13.s.s1.line.2: Case where A is not chosen: 3 must be chosen from the other 9, so there are C(9,2) ways.
z-m-28-13.s.s1.line.3: The case where A is chosen and the case where A is not chosen do not overlap and cover all the cases without missing any, so C(10,3)=C(9,2)+C(9,2).
z-m-28-13.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. If A is not chosen, all 3 must be chosen from the other 9 people, so it is C(9,3). The explanation in line 4 that 'they do not overlap and cover everything without missing any' is correct. But the value in line 3 is wrong, so the equation in the conclusion is wrong.
z-m-28-13.s.s2.prompt: Write out in 3 to 5 sentences, for a friend who missed class, why C(10,3)=C(9,2)+C(9,3) holds. Do not just show by calculating that the values are the same; include why the two cases do not overlap and why they cover all the cases without missing any.
z-m-28-13.s.s2.hint.0: What your friend does not know is 'why we add' and 'why C(9,2) and C(9,3).' First write one sentence for each.
z-m-28-13.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one particular person A, and ask for any case of choosing 3 people whether A was chosen or not.
z-m-28-13.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you base it on one particular person?
z-m-28-13.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the two cases cannot happen at the same time?
z-m-28-13.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say that every case falls into one of the two?
z-m-28-13.s.s2.selfAssess.3: Did you put into words the symbols your friend does not know?
z-m-28-13.s.s2.model.0: Fix one particular person A. The case where A is chosen only needs 2 more chosen from the other 9, so C(9,2) ways, and the case where A is not chosen needs 3 chosen from the 9, so C(9,3) ways. A person being chosen and not being chosen cannot happen at the same time, so they do not overlap, and every case is one of the two, so they cover everything without missing any. So adding the two values gives the total C(10,3).
z-m-28-13.s.s2.model.1: Divide the ways to choose 3 of 10 people into two groups: the 3-person teams with A in them and the 3-person teams without A. For a team with A, you only decide 2 people other than A from the 9, and for a team without A, you decide 3 of the 9. No team can both have A and not have A, so they do not overlap, and every team is one of the two, so the count has no omissions.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.prompt: If we apply the same method to 'the number of ways to choose 5 out of 12 people, C(12,5),' what is it equal to?
z-m-28-13.s.s3.hint.0: When choosing 5 of 12 people, write out of how many people and how many are chosen in the case where A is chosen and in the case where A is not chosen.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the pair of numbers in each option, one by one, with the two cases you wrote earlier.
z-m-28-13.s.s3.explain: If A is chosen, 4 more are chosen from the other 11, so it is C(11,4), and if A is not chosen, 5 are chosen from 11, so it is C(11,5). The two cases do not overlap and have no omissions, so we add. The value is 330+462=792=C(12,5).
